passage: Rain kept the boys indoors, and toys lay everywhere in Abebe's room. Abebe's aunt said they could have a story once the floor was clear. Emeka groaned and lay flat on the rug. Abebe thought, then held up one finger. "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." "Deal," said Emeka, sitting up. Abebe rolled the cars into a crate and counted them aloud. Emeka stacked the books on the low shelf. When they finished, they flopped down and opened the book about the tortoise.

qa.a: Abebe said, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story."

qa.q: How did Emeka feel about clearing up at the start, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Emeka felt reluctant. Emeka groaned and lay flat on the rug.

qa.q: What other approach could work if Emeka had refused the deal, and why?
qa.a: Abebe could turn the clearing into a race or a shop game. Play can make a chore feel lighter.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Emeka?
qa.a: Emeka gets a clear, fair share of the work and a story to look forward to. That is why sitting up and saying "Deal" makes sense.

grounding: A child splits the tidying between two children and names a story as the reward.

passage: At clean-up time in the kindergarten, Anjali looked at the mess and then at Rajni ma'am. "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story?" Rajni ma'am laughed. "Deal." Anjali zoomed each car into the car box. Rajni ma'am shelved the books. Soon the floor was clear, and Anjali ran to pick the story. "This one!"

qa.q: What did Anjali offer to do?
qa.a: She offered to do the cars.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she ran to pick the story?
qa.a: She was excited and happy that the job was done and the story was coming.

qa.q: What else could Anjali try with a classmate?
qa.a: The same deal, splitting the work and naming a fun reward at the end.

qa.q: How does Anjali's deal look to Rajni ma'am?
qa.a: Rajni ma'am finds it clever and fair, so she laughs and agrees.

grounding: A child splits the tidying with her teacher and names a story as the reward, which gets the work moving.

passage: I'm Madhav, and Sunaina is my little sister. On Saturday Mumma told us to tidy. Sunaina looked at the pile and said, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." I nearly said no, but it sounded fair. She did every car. I did the books. Then she climbed on my bed with a story. I don't know if she planned it or just wanted the story.

qa.q: What did Sunaina offer to do?
qa.a: She offered to do the cars.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he nearly said no?
qa.a: Madhav was unsure and a bit reluctant, but the deal seemed fair.

qa.q: What could Sunaina add to make the deal even better?
qa.a: She could let Madhav choose the story, so he gets something he wants too.

qa.q: How does the story at the end feel to Sunaina?
qa.a: She seems happy and satisfied, climbing on the bed straight away.

grounding: An older sibling describes a little sister splitting the tidying and naming a story as the reward, which gets the work done.
